description.en: The band close grip push-up adds a resistance band wrapped across the back during a close grip push-up. The band provides accommodating resistance, getting harder near the lockout where the triceps are strongest. The narrow hand position emphasizes the triceps over the chest.

en: Wrap a resistance band across your upper back, holding the ends in your hands.
Get into a push-up position with hands closer than shoulder-width.
Position your hands directly under your shoulders.
Brace your core and keep your body in a straight line.
Bend your elbows to lower your chest toward the floor.
Keep your elbows tucked close to your ribs.
Press through your hands to drive back up.
Lock out the elbows at the top against the band tension.
Builds triceps strength
Accommodating resistance overloads the lockout
Easy to scale by changing band tension
Develops chest and triceps together
Strong tricep finisher
No bench needed

description.en: The band one arm standing low row is a unilateral row using a low anchored band. The lifter stands facing the anchor and pulls the band with one hand, driving the elbow back. The single arm work isolates one lat at a time.

en: Anchor a resistance band low to a sturdy point.
Stand facing the anchor with feet shoulder width.
Grip the band with one hand and step back to take tension.
Brace your core and set a slight forward lean.
Pinch the shoulder blade down.
Pull the band back driving the elbow past the body.
Squeeze the lat hard at the top.
Lower with control to the start. Complete reps and switch sides.
Strong unilateral back builder
Constant band tension
No machine needed
Builds the lats
Strong band move
Useful at-home back move

description.en: The band single leg reverse calf raise is a unilateral tibialis anterior builder. The lifter sits or stands with a band looped around the toes of one foot and the other end anchored low in front. The lifter pulls the toes up toward the shin against the band.

en: Anchor a resistance band low in front of you.
Loop the other end around the toes of one foot.
Sit on a bench or stand against a wall.
Set the heel on the floor with the band taking tension.
Brace your core and keep the leg fixed.
Pull the toes up toward the shin against the band.
Squeeze the front of the shin hard at the top.
Lower with control. Complete reps and switch legs.
Strong shin builder
Useful for runners
Builds tibialis size
Trains ankle dorsiflexion
Strong band move
Useful for shin splints

description.en: The band standing leg curl uses a resistance band looped around the ankle and anchored to a low point. Standing on one leg, you curl the working leg up by flexing the knee against band tension. The standing position is functional and the band provides constant tension throughout the range.

en: Anchor a resistance band to a low point such as the bottom of a power rack.
Loop the other end of the band around your right ankle.
Stand facing the anchor with feet shoulder-width apart.
Step back to create tension in the band.
Brace your core and stand tall, holding onto something for balance if needed.
Curl your right heel up toward your glutes by bending the knee.
Squeeze your hamstring at the top of the curl.
Lower your foot back down with control. Complete reps, then switch legs.
Trains hamstrings without a machine
Constant band tension through the range
Standing position is functional
Single-leg work corrects imbalances
Practical for home training
Easy to scale by changing band tension

description.en: The barbell clean deadlift is a deadlift variation performed with the grip width and posture of a clean. It is used as a technique developer for the first pull of the clean, training the proper bar path and posture without the explosive second pull. It is also a great strength-builder for the posterior chain.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart. The barbell should be just above your feet.
Grip the bar with a clean grip — slightly wider than shoulder-width, hook grip if comfortable.
Set up: hips slightly higher than knees, chest up, shoulders directly over the bar (or slightly in front), back flat. Brace your core.
Lift the bar by extending your knees first, maintaining the chest-up position.
Keep the bar close to your shins and thighs throughout the pull.
Continue lifting until you stand fully upright with the bar at thigh level.
Reverse the motion: hinge hips back, slide bar down legs, return to floor.
Maintain control throughout. This is a strength and technique exercise — not explosive.
Trains the first pull of the clean
Builds posterior chain strength
Develops proper bar path
Useful for Olympic lift technique work
Easier on the wrists than a clean
Great strength accessory

description.en: The barbell complex stiff leg deadlift clean step is an Olympic-style barbell complex linking three movements without dropping the bar. Starting with a stiff leg deadlift, transitioning to a power clean, then adding a step pattern, the complex builds explosive strength, conditioning, and Olympic lifting skill all in one continuous flow.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart, the bar on the floor in front of you.
Begin with a stiff leg deadlift, lifting the bar to standing.
Lower the bar to mid-thigh.
From mid-thigh, perform a power clean to the front rack position.
Catch the bar in the front rack with elbows high.
Step forward into a lunge while maintaining the front rack.
Drive back to standing.
Lower the bar back to the floor. That sequence is one rep.
Trains multiple lifts in one continuous flow
Strong conditioning and metabolic demand
Builds Olympic lifting skill
Develops explosive total body strength
Time-efficient compound training
Useful for off-season athletes

description.en: The barbell incline bench press is a pressing exercise performed on a bench inclined at roughly 30 to 45 degrees. The angle biases the clavicular (upper) head of the pectoralis major and the anterior deltoid, making it one of the most important exercises for developing a complete, balanced chest. It is a staple of bodybuilding and powerlifting accessory work.

en: Set an adjustable bench or use a fixed incline bench at roughly 30 to 45 degrees. 30 degrees biases the chest most; steeper angles bias the shoulders.
Lie back on the bench with your eyes directly under the bar. Plant both feet firmly on the floor.
Grip the bar with hands slightly wider than shoulder-width. Wrap your thumbs around the bar.
Pull your shoulder blades down and back into the bench, lift your chest, and brace your core.
Unrack the bar with straight arms and bring it over your upper chest. Take a deep breath in.
Lower the bar under control to your upper chest, allowing your elbows to flare to roughly 45 to 75 degrees from your torso.
Press the bar back up and slightly toward your face, finishing with arms locked out over your upper chest. Exhale as you press.
Rack the bar safely with the help of a spotter when working near maximum loads.
Most effective barbell exercise for developing the upper (clavicular) chest
Builds the front deltoids and triceps heavily as secondary movers
Allows progressive overload across years of training
Carries over to flat bench press strength
Excellent benchmark for upper-body pressing strength
Easily programmed for hypertrophy or strength

description.en: The barbell rollout from bench is an anti-extension core exercise where you kneel behind a bench with a loaded barbell on the floor in front of you. You roll the barbell forward along the floor while bracing your core, then pull it back. The bench provides a stopping reference point.

en: Kneel behind a flat bench. Place a loaded barbell (or just the bar) on the floor in front of the bench.
Grip the bar with both hands, shoulder-width apart.
Brace your core hard. Tuck your pelvis.
Roll the barbell forward, extending your body. The bar rolls under or past the bench.
Continue until your body is extended as far as your core can hold without arching your back.
Pull the barbell back to start by contracting your abs and lats.
Do not let your lower back arch at any point.
Aim for 8 to 12 reps per set.
Builds anti-extension core strength
Barbell allows heavier loading than ab wheel
Bench provides reference point for range
Develops lat and shoulder strength
No ab wheel needed — just a barbell
Scalable by range of motion and bar weight

description.en: The barbell standing reverse grip curl is performed with an overhand (pronated) grip rather than the standard underhand grip. The pronated grip shifts emphasis from the biceps to the brachioradialis and forearm extensors, building forearm size and grip strength while still working the biceps.

en: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart.
Hold a barbell at thigh level with palms facing back (overhand grip).
Pin your elbows against your sides.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Curl the bar up by bending at the elbows while maintaining the overhand grip.
Continue until the bar is near shoulder height.
Squeeze the forearms and biceps at the top.
Lower the bar back down with control to full extension.
Targets brachioradialis and forearm extensors
Builds forearm size and grip
Different stimulus than standard curls
Useful for thicker arms
Pairs well with regular curls
Strong wrist stability work

description.en: The barbell standing wide-grip biceps curl uses a wider-than-shoulder-width grip on the barbell to shift emphasis to the short (inner) head of the biceps brachii. The wide grip is one of the most effective ways to target the bicep peak. It is a simple variation that adds significant variety to standard barbell curls.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Grip a barbell with an underhand grip wider than shoulder-width — roughly 1.25 to 1.5 times shoulder-width.
Let the bar hang at arm’s length in front of your thighs.
Pin your elbows to your sides. Brace your core.
Curl the bar up by bending only at the elbows. The wide grip naturally turns your wrists slightly outward.
Continue until the bar reaches shoulder height. Squeeze your biceps hard at the top.
Lower under control over two seconds.
Do not swing or use body english.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Emphasizes the short (inner) head of the biceps
Builds bicep peak development
Different stimulus than standard or close-grip curls
Easy variation that adds significant variety
Builds bicep size effectively
Useful for breaking through bicep plateaus

description.en: The barbell Zercher carry holds a barbell in the crook of your elbows (Zercher position) and walks for distance. The front-loaded position challenges the biceps, core anti-flexion, and upper back. It is named after Ed Zercher and builds tremendous core and arm endurance.

en: Set a barbell at hip height in a rack. Step into the bar and cradle it in the crooks of your elbows.
Clasp your hands together in front of you. The bar rests in your elbow creases.
Stand up with the bar. Pull your shoulders back. Chest tall.
Brace your core hard — the bar pulls you forward.
Walk forward with controlled strides.
Maintain upright posture throughout.
Walk for the desired distance. Use padding on the bar for elbow comfort.
Use moderate weight. Aim for 30 to 60 seconds per set.
Builds anti-flexion core strength
Develops bicep and forearm endurance
Trains upper back posture under load
Unique loaded carry variation
Builds total-body conditioning
Named after strongman Ed Zercher

description.en: The bodyweight narrow stance squat is performed with the feet positioned closer than shoulder-width. The narrow stance shifts emphasis from the glutes and inner thighs to the quadriceps, especially the outer quad fibers. It is a strong quad-focused option for home training or warm-up.

en: Stand with feet narrower than shoulder-width, almost together.
Hold your arms out in front for balance.
Brace your core and stand tall.
Squat down by bending your knees and hips.
Keep your knees tracking over your toes.
Allow your torso to lean slightly forward as you descend for balance.
Continue down until your thighs are parallel to the floor or as deep as mobility allows.
Drive up through your heels to stand back to the starting position.
Maximally targets the quadriceps
Outer quad emphasis with narrow stance
Builds quad size with no equipment
Useful for home training or warm-up
Improves ankle and knee mobility
Foundation for harder single-leg variations

description.en: The bottle weighted alternate front raise uses two filled water bottles as makeshift weights to perform alternating front raises. The lifter raises one bottle in front to shoulder height, lowers, then raises the other. It is a strong shoulder builder for home workouts.

en: Hold a filled water bottle in each hand at the sides.
Stand with the feet hip width apart.
Brace your core and keep the back straight.
Raise one bottle straight in front to shoulder height.
Keep the arm slightly bent and the wrist neutral.
Lower the bottle with control to the side.
Repeat with the opposite arm in alternating fashion.
Continue alternating until done.
No weights needed
Trains the front delts
Strong home option
Useful shoulder builder
Builds shoulder shape

description.en: The bottle weighted bent over row substitutes filled water bottles for dumbbells in a standard bent over row. The lifter hinges forward and rows both bottles to the lower ribs. It is a useful home option when no real weights are available.

en: Hold a filled water bottle in each hand at the sides.
Stand with the feet hip width apart and knees soft.
Hinge at the hips until the torso is near horizontal.
Let the arms hang straight down toward the floor.
Brace your core and keep the back flat.
Pull both bottles up to the lower ribs.
Squeeze the lats and upper back at the top.
Lower with control to the start.
No weights needed
Builds the back
Trains the biceps
Strong home option
Useful back builder

description.en: The cable incline cross rear fly is performed face-down on an incline bench while holding cables that cross in front of the body. The arms sweep out and back in a reverse fly motion. The bench support and crossed-cable setup nail the rear delts with constant tension and zero momentum.

en: Set an incline bench between two low cable pulleys.
Lie face-down on the bench with feet on the floor.
Reach down and grab the right cable with your left hand and the left cable with your right hand.
Start with the cables crossed under your chest.
Brace your core and pin your chest to the bench.
Sweep your arms out and back to your sides.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the end range.
Return slowly to the crossed position.
Strict rear delt isolation
Constant cable tension
No momentum or torso swing
Bench-supported for strict form
Builds rear delt detail
Useful for shoulder balance

description.en: The cable low seated row is a seated cable row where the pulley is positioned at the lowest possible point, creating a steeper upward pulling angle. This angle emphasizes the lower lats and builds back thickness. It is essentially a standard seated row with the cable set lower.

en: Set a cable to the lowest position. Sit on a bench or the floor facing the cable.
Grip a V-bar, rope, or straight bar handle.
Sit upright with feet on footplates or flat on the floor.
Row the handle toward your lower abdomen by driving your elbows back.
The low cable angle creates a slightly upward pulling path.
Squeeze your lats and lower back at the end of the row.
Slowly extend forward.
Aim for 10 to 12 reps per set.
Low angle emphasizes the lower lats
Builds back thickness
Constant cable tension
Easy to load progressively
Different angle than standard seated row
Comfortable seated position

description.en: The cable lying Pallof press is performed lying on the floor with a cable handle held at the chest. Pressing the handle straight up while resisting the lateral pull of the cable trains pure anti-rotation core strength. The lying position eliminates standing balance demands and isolates the core fully.

en: Set a cable to chest height when lying down (low pulley typically works).
Lie on your back perpendicular to the cable station.
Hold a single handle at your chest with both hands, palms together.
Position the cable to your side so it pulls laterally on your hands.
Brace your core hard against the lateral pull.
Press the handle straight up over your chest until your arms are extended.
Hold the press for one count while resisting the cable pull.
Bring the handle back to your chest with control. Complete reps, then switch sides.
Pure anti-rotation core training
Lying position eliminates balance demands
Builds core stability under lateral force
Strong oblique engagement
Useful for athletes who need rotational stability
Easy to scale by changing cable resistance

description.en: Child's Pose (Balasana in Sanskrit) is a foundational resting yoga pose performed kneeling on the floor with the hips sitting back over the heels and the torso folded forward. It gently lengthens the lower back, hips, and ankles while calming the nervous system, making it one of the most useful recovery poses in yoga and a popular cool-down stretch.

en: Kneel on the floor with your big toes touching and your knees roughly hip-width apart (or wider for a deeper hip stretch).
Sit your hips back onto your heels. If your hips do not reach your heels, place a folded blanket or pillow between them for support.
Walk your hands forward and lower your torso between or over your thighs. Rest your forehead on the floor or a block if it does not reach.
Extend your arms straight out in front of you with your palms down (active version), or rest them alongside your body with palms up (passive, restorative version).
Relax your shoulders away from your ears and let your chest sink toward the floor. Breathe slowly into your back ribs.
Hold for 30 seconds to several minutes, breathing deeply throughout.
To come out, walk your hands back toward your body and slowly sit up on your heels.
Gently stretches the lower back, hips, thighs, and ankles
Calms the nervous system and helps reduce stress and anxiety
Decompresses the spine after standing, sitting, or backbends
Excellent recovery pose between more demanding yoga postures
Encourages slow, deep breathing into the back body

musclesWorked: Quadriceps and tops of the feet

description.en: The chin tuck is a postural correction exercise that retracts the chin straight back, strengthening the deep cervical flexors and stretching the suboccipital muscles. It is the gold-standard exercise for correcting forward head posture and is widely prescribed in physical therapy.

en: Sit or stand tall with good posture. Look straight ahead.
Without tilting your head up or down, pull your chin straight back — like making a double chin.
Imagine someone is pushing your chin straight back into your spine.
Hold for 5 to 10 seconds. You should feel a stretch at the base of your skull.
Release and relax.
Repeat 10 to 15 times.
The movement is small — only 1 to 2 inches of retraction.
Can be performed against a wall for tactile feedback.
Gold-standard for correcting forward head posture
Strengthens deep cervical flexors
Stretches suboccipital muscles
Widely prescribed in physical therapy
No equipment needed
Can be done anywhere, anytime

musclesWorked: Deep cervical flexors (longus colli, longus capitis)

description.en: The dumbbell Arnold press, named after Arnold Schwarzenegger, is a shoulder press variation that adds a rotation to the bottom and top of the lift. Starting with palms facing your body and rotating to palms facing forward at lockout, the movement recruits all three heads of the deltoid in a single rep — front, side, and rear — making it one of the most complete single-exercise shoulder builders.

en: Sit on a bench set upright with back support, or stand. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder level with palms facing your body (like the top of a bicep curl).
Your elbows should be in front of your body and the dumbbells held close to your shoulders.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Begin pressing the dumbbells overhead. As you press, rotate your wrists outward so that at lockout, your palms face forward.
At the top, your arms should be fully extended overhead with palms facing forward — the same finish position as a standard shoulder press.
Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbells while rotating your palms back toward your body.
Finish the descent with palms facing your body and elbows in front of your torso.
The rotation should be smooth and continuous throughout the press, not abrupt at the top or bottom.
Recruits all three heads of the deltoid in a single rep (front, side, rear)
Builds shoulder size and strength with less load than a standard press
Improves shoulder mobility through the rotation pattern
Can be done seated or standing with light loads
Useful warm-up exercise for heavier shoulder pressing
Trains the rotator cuff dynamically through the rotation

musclesWorked: Posterior deltoid (less, but more than a standard press)

description.en: The dumbbell front squat is a front-loaded squat where you hold a dumbbell on each shoulder (or one in goblet position) to mimic the barbell front squat. The front-loaded position forces an upright torso and emphasizes the quads. It is excellent for at-home leg work without a barbell.

en: Stand with a dumbbell in each hand. Curl them up to your shoulders.
Rest the dumbbells on the front of your shoulders, with the dumbbell heads sitting on top of your shoulders. Keep elbows pointed forward and high.
Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly turned out.
Brace your core hard. Lift your chest.
Sit your hips straight down with an upright torso.
Descend until your hip crease drops below your knees.
Drive straight up through your full feet. Squeeze your glutes at the top.
Maintain perfect upright torso position throughout.
Builds quad-dominant squatting
Forces upright torso position
Easy to set up at home
No barbell needed
Develops core bracing
Excellent for beginners learning front squats

description.en: The dumbbell one arm wrist curl is performed seated with the forearm braced on a bench and a dumbbell in one hand. By flexing only at the wrist, you isolate the forearm flexors with strict form. Single-arm work allows mind-muscle focus and corrects strength imbalances.

en: Sit on a bench with feet flat on the floor.
Hold a dumbbell in your right hand with palm facing up.
Rest your right forearm on your right thigh with the wrist hanging off the knee.
Brace your core and sit tall.
Lower the dumbbell by extending your wrist down toward the floor.
Allow the dumbbell to roll back through your fingers slightly at the bottom.
Curl the dumbbell back up by flexing your wrist.
Squeeze your forearm at the top of the curl. Switch arms.
Strict single-arm forearm isolation
Builds grip strength
Corrects left-right imbalances
Allows progressive loading
Develops wrist flexion strength
Useful for athletes who need strong forearms

description.en: The dumbbell over bench one arm neutral wrist curl uses a neutral grip with the forearm braced over a bench. The neutral grip biases the brachioradialis and forearm extensors. It is a useful forearm builder.

en: Kneel beside a flat bench.
Hold a dumbbell in one hand with a neutral grip.
Rest the forearm flat on the bench with the wrist past the edge.
Hold the wrist with the opposite hand for stability.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Curl the dumbbell upward by raising the wrist.
Squeeze the forearm hard at the top.
Lower with control. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Builds the forearms
Strong neutral grip move
Trains the brachioradialis
Useful for grip
Builds wrist strength

description.en: The dumbbell overhead lunge holds a dumbbell locked out overhead in each hand while performing walking lunges. The overhead position demands serious shoulder stability and core bracing while the lunges build single-leg strength.

en: Press two dumbbells overhead. Arms fully extended, biceps by your ears.
Stand with feet hip-width apart. Brace your core hard.
Step forward into a lunge with your right foot. Lower your left knee toward the floor.
Maintain the overhead lockout — arms should not drift forward.
Drive through your right foot. Step forward with your left foot into the next lunge.
Continue walking for the desired distance.
Use light weight — overhead stability is the limiting factor.
Aim for 6 to 10 steps per leg.
Demands elite overhead stability
Builds total-body coordination
Develops single-leg strength under overhead load
Exposes shoulder weakness
Full-body compound exercise
Trains multi-planar stability

description.en: The dumbbell preacher hammer curl combines the strict isolation of the preacher bench with a hammer (neutral) grip. The preacher pad locks the upper arms in place while the neutral grip targets the brachialis and brachioradialis. The result is heavy isolation of the deeper arm muscles for thicker arms.

en: Sit at a preacher bench with the pad against your armpits.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand with palms facing each other (hammer grip).
Rest your upper arms on the preacher pad with arms extended down.
Pin your chest to the pad and brace your core.
Curl both dumbbells up by bending at the elbows, keeping the hammer grip.
Continue until your forearms are roughly vertical.
Squeeze your biceps and brachialis at the top.
Lower the dumbbells back down with control to a full stretch.
Strict isolation with the preacher pad
Hammer grip targets brachialis
Builds arm thickness and bicep peak
Eliminates body english
Useful for breaking through curl plateaus
Strong forearm engagement

description.en: The dumbbell renegade row is a compound exercise where you hold a plank on two dumbbells and row one dumbbell up to your hip while balancing on the other. It builds back strength, anti-rotation core stability, and shoulder endurance simultaneously. It differs from the plank push-up row in that it skips the push-up.

en: Place two hex dumbbells on the floor at shoulder width. Get into a high-plank position gripping the dumbbells.
Set your feet wider than hip-width for stability. Brace your core hard.
Form a straight body line from heels to head.
Row the right dumbbell up to your right hip by driving your elbow straight back. Squeeze your shoulder blade.
Keep your hips perfectly level throughout. Do not rotate or tilt.
Lower the right dumbbell under control. Then row the left dumbbell with the same form.
Continue alternating until you complete the desired total reps.
Use moderate weight — anti-rotation control matters more than load.
Builds back strength and anti-rotation core stability simultaneously
Trains the lats, rhomboids, and rear delts unilaterally
Develops shoulder and core endurance
Exposes left-right strength imbalances
Works at home with one pair of hex dumbbells
Time-efficient compound exercise

description.en: The dumbbell standing alternate Arnold press is the Arnold press performed standing one arm at a time. The standing position adds full body engagement while the alternating pattern adds anti-lateral-flexion core demand. The wrist rotation through the press hits all three deltoid heads.

en: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder level.
Start with palms facing your face (supinated grip), elbows tucked in front.
Brace your core hard.
Press the right dumbbell up while rotating your wrist outward to a pronated grip at lockout.
Lock out the right arm overhead while keeping the left dumbbell stationary at the shoulder.
Reverse the motion, rotating back to the supinated grip at the shoulder.
Repeat with the left arm. Alternate sides each rep.
Maintain a strong upright trunk throughout.
Hits all three deltoid heads
Adds anti-lateral-flexion core challenge
Standing position adds full body engagement
Single-arm version builds stability
Corrects left-right imbalances
Strong shoulder development variation

description.en: The dumbbell standing reverse curl is performed with an overhand (pronated) grip rather than the standard underhand grip. The pronated grip shifts emphasis from the biceps to the brachioradialis and forearm extensors, building forearm size and grip strength while still working the biceps.

en: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand at thigh level with palms facing back (overhand grip).
Pin your elbows against your sides.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Curl both dumbbells up by bending at the elbows while maintaining the overhand grip.
Continue until the dumbbells are near shoulder height.
Squeeze the forearms and biceps at the top.
Lower the dumbbells back down with control to full extension.
Targets forearm extensors and brachioradialis
Builds forearm size and grip
Different stimulus than standard curls
Useful for thicker arms
Pairs well with regular curls for full development
Strong wrist stability work

description.en: The EZ barbell incline triceps extension is a skull crusher done on an incline bench. The lifter lies on the incline and lowers the EZ bar to the forehead. The incline angle changes the tension on the long head of the triceps.

en: Set an incline bench at about thirty degrees.
Lie back on the incline holding an EZ curl bar.
Press the bar up overhead to lockout.
Brace your core and keep the back against the bench.
Lower the bar by bending the elbows.
Bring the bar down toward the forehead.
Keep the elbows pointing up.
Press the bar back up to lockout.
Trains the triceps
Strong skull crusher variation
Builds the long head
Useful for arm size
Builds the upper arms

description.en: The EZ barbell standing back wrist curl is a wrist curl done with the bar held behind the back. The lifter stands tall and curls the wrists up. The behind the back position trains the forearm flexors at a unique angle.

en: Hold an EZ curl bar behind the back at hip level.
Stand with the feet hip width apart.
Set the hands shoulder width apart on the bar.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Let the bar hang down with the wrists relaxed.
Curl the wrists up by flexing the forearms.
Squeeze the forearms hard at the top.
Lower with control to the start.
Trains the forearm flexors
Strong wrist builder
Behind the back angle
Useful for grip
Builds the forearms

description.en: The floor crunch feet on bench is a basic crunch done with the feet elevated on a flat bench. The bent knee feet up position locks the lower body and isolates the abs. It is a useful introductory ab builder.

en: Lie on the floor in front of a flat bench.
Place the feet up on top of the bench with knees bent.
Set the hands lightly behind the head.
Brace your core and keep the lower back on the floor.
Curl the head and shoulders up off the floor.
Squeeze the abs hard at the top.
Hold briefly at the peak.
Lower with control to the start.
Builds the core
Strong basic crunch
Useful for beginners
Trains the abs
No equipment needed

description.en: The forward jump is a plyometric exercise where you perform repeated standing long jumps in succession, jumping forward without resetting. The continuous nature builds power endurance, conditioning, and explosive strength simultaneously. It is more demanding than single-rep broad jumps.

en: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart at a starting line.
Sit hips back, swing arms, and explosively jump forward as far as you can.
Land softly with bent knees and weight slightly forward.
Immediately load again and jump forward into the next rep.
Continue jumping forward for the desired number of reps (5 to
or distance.
Each jump should be near-maximum effort. Do not let fatigue compromise the jump distance.
Walk back to the start to rest. Rest 60 to 90 seconds between sets.
Perform 3 to 5 sets per session.
Builds power endurance and conditioning
Develops explosive strength under fatigue
More demanding than single broad jumps
Excellent athletic carryover
No equipment needed
Burns calories at a high rate

description.en: The handboard hang with 135 degree elbow is a climbing isometric drill done with the arms only slightly bent. The position challenges grip while loading the lats and biceps in a stretched range.

en: Reach up and grab a hangboard with both hands.
Use a deep edge or jug for the grip.
Pull up so the elbows form a 135 degree angle.
Brace the core and keep the body still.
Hold the position with the slight arm bend.
Engage the lats and biceps to maintain the hold.
Continue the isometric for the working time.
Lower with control to the start.
Builds grip strength.
Trains the lats and biceps near full extension.
Climbing specific drill.
Useful for pulling endurance.
Builds the upper back.

description.en: The hanging knee circle raise is a hanging abs move that traces a circular motion with the knees. The lifter hangs from a bar, raises the knees to chest height, and circles them around in a wide arc. The circle motion hits the abs and obliques together.

en: Hang from a pull up bar with hands at shoulder width.
Brace your core hard.
Raise the knees up toward the chest.
Begin tracing a circular motion with the knees.
Move the knees up to one side then around to the bottom.
Continue around to the other side and back to the top.
Complete a full circle with the knees.
Reverse direction for the next rep.
Strong oblique builder
Trains rotational core
Builds the abs
Useful core finisher
Builds the rectus abdominis
Strong hanging move

description.en: The inverted row (body row or Australian pull-up) hangs from a bar at hip height and pulls the chest toward the bar. It is the bodyweight pulling counterpart to the push-up and is the primary back exercise for those who cannot do pull-ups.

en: Set a bar at about hip height. Lie underneath and grip with overhand grip.
Extend your body in a straight line from heels to head. Heels on the floor.
Pull your chest toward the bar by driving elbows back.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top.
Lower under control.
Adjust body angle for difficulty — more horizontal is harder.
Aim for 8 to 15 reps.
Progress toward pull-ups by lowering the bar height over time.
Primary bodyweight back exercise
Counterpart to the push-up
Adjustable difficulty by body angle
Builds pulling strength toward pull-ups
No pull-up bar height needed
Accessible for all levels

description.en: The jack jump is a more explosive version of the standard jumping jack, where you jump higher and emphasize the explosive arm-and-leg spreading motion. It builds power, cardiovascular conditioning, and coordination simultaneously.

en: Stand tall with feet together, arms at your sides.
Jump up explosively. While airborne, spread your feet wide and raise your arms overhead.
Land softly with feet wider than shoulder-width and arms overhead.
Immediately jump back to the starting position with feet together and arms at sides.
Continue rapidly. Each jump should be more explosive than a standard jumping jack.
Stay on the balls of your feet. Land softly with bent knees.
Perform for time (20 to 45 seconds) per set.
Increase tempo for more cardiovascular demand.
Builds explosive lower-body power
Excellent cardiovascular conditioning
Improves coordination
No equipment needed
Easy warm-up or HIIT exercise
Increases heart rate rapidly

description.en: The leg pull (also called Pilates leg pull) is a reverse-plank variation where you support yourself on your hands and feet face-up and alternately lift one leg straight up toward the ceiling. It is essentially identical to the reverse plank with leg lift. It builds posterior chain strength, hip control, and core engagement.

en: Sit on the floor with legs extended in front and hands placed behind you, fingers pointing toward your feet.
Press into your hands and heels to lift your hips up. Body forms a straight line from heels to head.
Squeeze your glutes hard. Drive your hips up.
From this reverse plank, lift your right leg straight up toward the ceiling.
Keep your hips perfectly still — they should not drop on the lifting side.
Hold the leg lifted for 1 to 2 seconds.
Lower the right leg and immediately lift the left.
Continue alternating for 8 to 12 reps per side.
Builds posterior chain strength
Develops core anti-rotation
Trains glute and hamstring control
Improves shoulder stability
No equipment needed
Useful Pilates exercise for core integration

description.en: The lying back extension is a bodyweight back-strengthening move performed face down on the floor. The chest and arms lift off the ground in a controlled extension. It is a core-friendly version of the hyperextension that requires no equipment and is suitable for home training.

en: Lie face down on the floor with legs extended and arms in front.
Rest your forehead lightly on the ground.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes.
Lift your chest, arms, and legs off the floor at the same time.
Continue lifting until you feel a strong contraction in the lower back.
Hold the top position briefly.
Lower back down with control.
Reset and repeat.
Builds lower back strength
Strengthens the posterior chain
No equipment required
Useful for home training
Reduces lower back pain over time
Improves posture

description.en: The lever seated squat is performed in a seated position on a machine, with the back fully supported. By eliminating standing balance and lower back demands, the machine isolates the quads heavily. It is an excellent choice for direct quad work or for lifters with back limitations.

en: Sit on the seat of the lever seated squat machine.
Place your back firmly against the back pad.
Position your feet on the platform shoulder-width apart.
Grip the handles for stability.
Unrack the safety and brace your core.
Squat the platform away by bending your knees.
Continue until your thighs are roughly perpendicular to the platform.
Drive through your heels to extend your legs back to the starting position. Re-rack the safety.
Heavy quad loading with full back support
Eliminates balance demands
Reduces lower back stress
Allows progressive heavy weight
Useful for lifters with back limitations
Builds quad size and strength

description.en: The plank push-up row is a full-body combination exercise where you perform a push-up holding two dumbbells, then row each dumbbell up to your hip while staying in the plank position. The combined push-pull-stabilize movement trains the chest, back, shoulders, triceps, biceps, and core in one rep — making it one of the most efficient upper-body exercises in any program.

en: Place a pair of hexagonal dumbbells on the floor. Hex dumbbells are essential — round ones will roll.
Get into a high-plank position gripping the dumbbells with hands directly under your shoulders. Set feet wider than hip-width for stability.
Brace your core hard and form a straight body line from heels to head.
Perform a push-up by lowering your chest toward the dumbbells, then pressing back up to the high-plank.
At the top of the push-up, row the right dumbbell up to your right hip by driving your elbow straight back. Squeeze your shoulder blade.
Keep your hips perfectly level throughout the row — do not rotate or tilt. This is the hardest part.
Lower the right dumbbell back to the floor under control. Then row the left dumbbell with the same form.
That is one full rep. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use moderate weight — form matters more than load.
Trains push, pull, and core stability in one movement
Builds the chest, back, shoulders, triceps, biceps, and core simultaneously
Develops anti-rotation core strength
Time-efficient combination of multiple exercises
Exposes left-right strength imbalances on the row
Works at home with one pair of hex dumbbells

description.en: The plyo side lunge stretch combines a deep side lunge with a plyometric switch jump. From a deep lateral lunge on one side, you push off explosively and jump laterally into a deep lunge on the other side. The combination builds power, lateral mobility, and adductor strength.

en: Stand tall with feet wider than shoulder-width apart.
Shift your weight to your right leg into a deep side lunge.
Bend the right knee and push your hips back.
Keep the left leg extended out to the side with foot flat.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Push off explosively with the right leg.
Jump laterally to the left leg into a deep side lunge on the other side.
Continue alternating sides with explosive jumps.
Builds lower body power
Improves lateral mobility
Strong adductor and glute work
Combines mobility with plyometrics
No equipment required
Useful for athletic conditioning

description.en: The prayer push is a static isometric exercise that presses the palms together hard at chest height in a prayer position. The forceful press engages the chest and inner pec fibers isometrically while stretching the wrists. It is also used as an upper body mobility drill.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart.
Bring your palms together in front of your chest in a prayer position.
Press the bases of the palms together firmly.
Pull the elbows out to the sides at chest level.
Press the palms together hard, engaging the chest.
Hold the maximum chest contraction.
Maintain steady deep breathing through the hold.
Release the press, rest briefly, and repeat for desired sets.
Isometric chest activation
Stretches the wrists
No equipment required
Strong inner chest engagement
Useful for warmups
Builds mind-muscle connection

description.en: Push-ups are the most fundamental bodyweight upper-body exercise. You hold a high plank and lower your chest to the floor, then press back up. This page covers the standard push-up as a separate entry from other push-up variations on the site.

en: Get into a high plank. Hands slightly wider than shoulder-width, fingers forward.
Set your body in a straight line from heels to head.
Lower your chest to the floor by bending at the elbows.
Keep your elbows at about 45 degrees to your body.
Touch your chest to the floor (or come within an inch).
Press back up to lockout.
Maintain a straight body line throughout.
Aim for 10 to 25 reps per set depending on fitness level.
Most fundamental bodyweight pressing exercise
No equipment needed
Builds chest, tricep, and shoulder strength
Develops core stability
Can be done anywhere
Endlessly scalable through variations

description.en: The resistance band kneeling leg half circle on bench is a glute drill done from a quadruped position braced over a bench. Pressing the banded leg in a half circle path loads the glute through extension and abduction at once.

en: Loop a resistance band around one foot.
Anchor the band end to a low fixed point.
Set up on hands and knees with the chest supported on a bench.
Brace the core and keep the back flat.
Lift the banded leg off the floor with the knee bent.
Press the foot back and up against the band.
Sweep the leg out to the side in a half circle.
Return with control and continue for all reps then switch.
Builds the glute through multiple ranges.
Loads extension and abduction.
Bench keeps the back stable.
Useful glute accessory.
Joint friendly drill.

description.en: The resistance band seated face pull is a seated version of the classic face pull using a resistance band. The lifter sits and anchors a band at chest height, then pulls the band toward the face with elbows high. It is a strong upper back posture builder.

en: Anchor a resistance band at chest height to a sturdy point.
Sit on a bench or the floor facing the anchor.
Grip the band with both hands at the ends or with a rope attachment.
Set the arms straight out in front taking tension.
Brace your core and pinch the shoulder blades.
Pull the band toward the face with elbows high.
Stop with the hands at the sides of the face and elbows above shoulders.
Squeeze the rear delts hard. Lower with control.
Strong rear delt builder
Trains upper back posture
No machine needed
Useful posture builder
Strong band move
Builds shoulder health

description.en: The roll ball biceps brachii is a self myofascial release drill for the front of the upper arm. Pressing a small ball against the biceps and rolling slowly releases knots from heavy curling and pulling work.

en: Stand next to a wall with a massage ball in one hand.
Place the ball against the front of the upper arm.
Press the arm into the wall with the ball trapped between.
Brace the core and stay tall.
Roll the biceps slowly over the ball.
Pause on tender spots for several breaths.
Cover the full length of the upper arm.
Continue for the working time then switch sides.
Releases the biceps.
Reduces upper arm tightness.
Improves elbow mobility.
Useful after pulling work.
Joint friendly release.

description.en: The foot roll is a self-massage technique where you stand or sit with your foot on a small ball (lacrosse ball, tennis ball, or massage ball) and roll the bottom of your foot. It releases tightness in the plantar fascia and is one of the most effective interventions for plantar fasciitis, foot pain, and improving overall mobility.

en: Place a small firm ball (lacrosse ball, tennis ball, or massage ball) on the floor.
Stand with your right foot on top of the ball. Place your hands on a wall or chair for balance.
Apply moderate pressure by transferring some of your bodyweight onto the ball.
Slowly roll your foot back and forth across the ball — from heel to toes.
Roll slowly. Pause on tender spots and apply gentle sustained pressure.
Roll the inner and outer parts of your foot as well.
Continue for 1 to 2 minutes per foot.
For less intensity, sit in a chair instead of standing.
Releases plantar fascia tightness
Most effective intervention for plantar fasciitis
Improves foot mobility and circulation
Helps reduce arch pain
Inexpensive — needs only a small ball
Easy to do anywhere

description.en: The roll tibialis anterior is a self-myofascial release drill that targets the tibialis anterior on the front of the shin. The lifter rolls the front of the lower leg over a foam roller. The move releases shin tightness and is useful for runners.

en: Place a foam roller on the floor.
Get into a quadruped position with one shin over the roller.
Set the front of the lower leg on top of the roller.
Support the upper body on the hands.
Brace your core and keep the back flat.
Roll the shin slowly over the roller from below the knee to the ankle.
Stop on tight spots and hold for several seconds.
Switch legs and repeat on the other shin.
Releases shin tightness
Useful for runners
Strong recovery move
Easy to add to any session
Builds lower leg mobility
Helps with shin splints

description.en: The seated groin stretch (also called Butterfly Stretch or Baddha Konasana) is performed sitting with the soles of the feet pressed together and knees dropping out to the sides. It targets the adductors, groin, and inner thighs. Adding a forward fold deepens the stretch significantly.

en: Sit on the floor with legs extended. Bend both knees and bring the soles of your feet together.
Let your knees drop out to the sides toward the floor. Pull your heels as close to your groin as comfortable.
Hold your feet with both hands. Sit up tall with chest lifted.
Feel the stretch through your inner thighs and groin.
To deepen the stretch, gently press your knees toward the floor with your elbows.
For an even deeper stretch, fold forward from the hips with a flat back. Reach your forehead toward your feet.
Hold for 30 to 60 seconds. Breathe deeply.
Avoid forcing your knees down — let gravity do the work over time.
Stretches the adductors and groin
Opens the hips for squats and wide-stance lifts
Improves hip flexibility over time
Calming and restorative pose
No equipment needed
Useful for athletes in sports with lateral movement

description.en: The single-leg stride jump is a unilateral plyometric drill where you bound forward on one leg, landing on the same leg and immediately bounding again. It is similar to running stride jumps but on a single leg, building single-leg power and athletic acceleration mechanics.

en: Stand on your right leg with knee slightly bent. Left leg lifted slightly behind.
Bound forward by pushing off explosively from your right leg.
Drive your left knee up and your arms forward for momentum.
Cover as much horizontal distance as possible during the bound.
Land back on your right leg with a bent knee to absorb the impact.
Immediately bound forward again on the same leg.
Continue bounding for 5 to 10 reps, then switch to the left leg.
Focus on horizontal distance, not just height.
Builds single-leg horizontal power
Develops sprint acceleration mechanics
Trains single-leg landing stability
Excellent for sprint athletes
No equipment needed
Time-efficient power exercise

description.en: The sled closer hack squat is performed on a sled-style hack squat machine with feet placed close together. The narrow stance shifts emphasis to the outer quad and vastus lateralis. It is a strong choice for sculpting the outer sweep of the thigh and adds variety to leg day.

en: Step into the hack squat sled and place your shoulders against the pads.
Position your feet on the platform with feet close together.
Release the safety handles and brace your core.
Lower yourself by bending the knees.
Sit your hips back as you descend.
Continue down until your thighs are at or just below parallel.
Drive through your heels and the balls of your feet to stand.
Lock the safeties at the top after the final rep.
Targets the outer quad sweep
Builds the vastus lateralis
Stable, guided machine path
Easy to load progressively
Reduces lower back strain
Useful for quad development

description.en: The weighted full squat with overhead press is the classic thruster movement, combining a deep front squat with an overhead press in one fluid rep. The drive out of the squat helps press the weight overhead, training the entire body. It is one of the toughest conditioning moves there is.

en: Stand tall holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder level.
Position the dumbbells with palms facing each other or forward.
Brace your core and keep your chest up.
Squat down by sitting your hips back and bending the knees.
Continue until your thighs are below parallel.
Drive up explosively through your heels.
Use the upward momentum to press the dumbbells straight overhead.
Lock out the arms at the top, then lower the dumbbells back to shoulder level for the next rep.
Trains the entire body
Brutal conditioning move
Builds explosive power
Time-efficient combo
Strong calorie burner
CrossFit staple
